title: Planning of hydropower projects
summary: This subchapter is largely Nepali policy and practice, and the figures to know exactly are the capacity classification thresholds (1 MW and 25 MW carry licensing consequences), the license durations, and which agency does what — the Department of Electricity Development licenses, the Nepal Electricity Authority buys. Understand why Nepal is dominated by run-of-river schemes and what that implies for dry-season output, because that single fact shapes every planning question about the country's power system.

sections.heading: Nepal's hydropower context
sections.body:
**The resource.** Nepal's rivers fall from the Himalaya to the Terai over a short horizontal distance, giving the combination that hydropower needs — **large head and reliable flow**.

| Figure | Value |
|---|---|
| **Theoretical potential** | About **83,000 MW** |
| **Technically and economically feasible** | About **42,000 MW** |
| Developed to date | A small fraction of the feasible potential |

The gap between theoretical and feasible potential reflects **access, geology, environmental and social constraints, and market** — a scheme in an inaccessible high valley with no transmission line and no buyer is not a resource in any practical sense.

**Why Nepal's schemes are overwhelmingly RUN-OF-RIVER**, and this is the fact that shapes everything else:

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Steep, narrow valleys** | A reservoir needs a wide valley to store useful volume; Nepal's are mostly narrow gorges |
| **Resettlement** | A reservoir in an inhabited valley displaces communities — the most contentious issue in Nepali project development |
| **Sedimentation** | Himalayan rivers carry extreme sediment loads, which would fill a reservoir's dead storage quickly |
| **Capital cost and time** | A dam and reservoir cost far more and take far longer than a diversion weir |
| **Environmental impact** | Inundation of forest and farmland, loss of river continuity |

**The consequence, and the central problem of Nepal's power system:**

> A **run-of-river plant generates in proportion to the river's flow**, and Nepal's rivers carry perhaps **five to ten times** as much water in the monsoon as in the dry season. So ROR output **falls sharply in winter**, exactly when demand for lighting and heating peaks.

That mismatch is why Nepal has historically had **surplus energy in the monsoon and deficit in winter**, why **import and export arrangements with India** matter so much, and why **storage and peaking projects** are the strategic priority despite their difficulty. It is the single most useful fact for answering any planning question about Nepali hydropower.

**Plant types:**

| Type | Character | Nepali examples of the class |
|---|---|---|
| **Run-of-river (ROR)** | **No storage**; generates on the instantaneous flow | The great majority of Nepal's plants |
| **Peaking run-of-river (PROR)** | A **small pondage** (a few hours' storage) allows generation to be concentrated in the **daily peak** | Increasingly the preferred model |
| **Storage (reservoir)** | **Seasonal storage**; regulates flow between monsoon and dry season | Kulekhani is the classic Nepali example |
| **Pumped storage** | Pumps water uphill using surplus off-peak energy, generates at peak | Under study; needs surplus energy to be worthwhile |
| Cascade | A series of plants on one river, each using the tailwater of the last | Efficient use of a river's total head |

**PROR deserves emphasis** because it is the practical compromise: a **pondage of a few hours** costs a fraction of a seasonal reservoir but lets the plant deliver its full capacity during the **evening peak**, when energy is most valuable, rather than a constant trickle through the day. It converts an energy-only plant into a **capacity** plant, which is what a system short of peaking power needs.

**Capacity classification (Nepal):**

| Class | Capacity | Licensing consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Micro** | **Below 100 kW** | — |
| **Mini** | **100 kW – 1 MW** | — |
| **Small** | **1 – 25 MW** | — |
| **Medium** | **25 – 100 MW** | — |
| **Large** | **Above 100 MW** | — |

**Two thresholds carry legal weight** and are worth memorising for that reason:

> **Below 1 MW: NO survey or generation license is required** under the Electricity Act — a deliberate simplification to encourage small and community schemes.
> **The 25 MW threshold** separates small from medium and affects the approval route and, historically, the incentives available.

**Micro-hydro's importance in Nepal is disproportionate to its capacity.** Thousands of micro-hydro plants, typically **5 to 100 kW**, serve villages far from the grid, promoted through the **Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC)**. Their engineering is simple — a small diversion, a canal, a forebay, a penstock and a **cross-flow turbine** — and their significance is that they are **built, owned and maintained by the community**, which is what makes them last.

sections.heading: Investigations and study stages
sections.body:
**The study stages**, each with a defined scope and cost accuracy:

| Stage | Purpose | Cost accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Reconnaissance** | Identify the scheme from maps and a site visit; screen alternatives | ± 40% |
| **Pre-feasibility** | Establish that the scheme is worth studying in detail; preliminary layout and economics | ± 25% |
| **Feasibility** | Establish technical, economic, environmental and financial viability; the basis of the investment decision | ± 15% |
| **Detailed design (tender design)** | Drawings and specifications for construction | ± 10% |

Each stage **spends more to reduce uncertainty**, and the discipline is to abandon an unpromising scheme early rather than carry it forward on optimism.

**The investigations required:**

| Investigation | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| **Hydrological** | The **flow duration curve**, design flood, low flow, and their reliability |
| **Topographical** | The head available, the alignment, the reservoir area-capacity |
| **Geological** | Rock type, structure, faults, weathering, slope stability |
| **Geotechnical** | Foundation and tunnelling conditions; rock mass quality |
| **Sediment** | Concentration, gradation, mineralogy — governs the settling basin and turbine wear |
| **Seismic** | Design earthquake; fault proximity |
| **Environmental and social** | Impacts, mitigation, resettlement, environmental release |
| **Power market** | Demand, tariff, transmission access, the PPA |
| Access | Roads, transport of heavy equipment |
| Construction materials | Aggregate, sand, water |

**In the Himalaya, GEOLOGY dominates the risk**, and it is worth saying why:

| Condition | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Young, tectonically active rock** | Highly **fractured and sheared**; low rock mass quality |
| **Active faults and thrust zones** | The Main Boundary and Main Central Thrusts cross the country |
| **Squeezing and swelling ground** | Tunnels deform inward after excavation, requiring heavy support |
| **High water inflow** into tunnels | Delays and grouting cost |
| **Slope instability** | Landslides affecting surface structures, canals and access roads |

**Under-investigating the geology is the leading cause of cost and time overrun on Nepali hydropower**, and the overruns are large — tunnel conditions worse than assumed can double a project's cost. That is the practical argument for spending on **exploratory drilling, adits and geophysics** at the feasibility stage: the cost of investigation is small against the cost of the surprise.

**Sediment investigation** deserves separate mention because it is often treated as secondary and is not. Himalayan sediment is **abundant, coarse and highly abrasive** (quartz-rich), and it can **destroy a turbine runner within a single monsoon** if the settling basin is inadequate. The investigation must establish not only the **concentration** but the **particle size distribution** and the **mineralogy** — because it is the hard quartz fraction above about 0.2 mm that does the damage.

**Hydrological investigation** and its difficulty in Nepal: most project sites are **ungauged**, so the flow record must be **transferred** from a gauged catchment by area or by regional relationships, with a correction for rainfall and elevation. The uncertainty in that transfer is substantial, and it propagates directly into the energy estimate and hence the project economics.

The standard approach: use the **Department of Hydrology and Meteorology** records from the nearest gauged station, apply a **catchment area ratio** with a rainfall correction, verify against any short-term measurement at the site, and state the uncertainty. Where possible, **install a gauge at the site early** — a two-year record at the site is worth far more than a longer record transferred from elsewhere.

sections.heading: Licensing, agencies and project development
sections.body:
**The legal framework:**

| Instrument | Governs |
|---|---|
| **Electricity Act 2049 (1992)** and **Electricity Rules 2050 (1993)** | Survey and generation licenses, royalties, PPAs |
| **Water Resources Act 2049 (1992)** | Water use rights and their priority |
| **Environment Protection Act 2076 (2019)** and Rules 2077 | IEE and EIA requirements |
| Forest Act 2076 | Clearance for use of forest land |
| Land Acquisition Act 2034 | Compulsory acquisition and compensation |
| Industrial Enterprises Act, Foreign Investment Act | Investment incentives and approvals |

**Water use priority** under the Water Resources Act is worth knowing, because it settles conflicts between users:

> **1. Drinking water and domestic use · 2. Irrigation · 3. Agricultural uses (livestock, fisheries) · 4. HYDROPOWER · 5. Industrial · 6. Navigation · 7. Recreational · 8. Other**

**Hydropower ranks FOURTH**, below drinking water and irrigation. So an existing irrigation intake or a village water supply has a **prior right**, and a hydropower project must accommodate it — which is a real constraint on many Nepali schemes and a source of local dispute.

**Licenses and the agencies that issue them:**

| License | Duration | Issued by |
|---|---|---|
| **Survey license** | **5 years** (extendable) | **Department of Electricity Development (DoED)** |
| **Generation license** | **Up to 35 years** (30 for projects with foreign investment) | **DoED** |
| Transmission and distribution licenses | As specified | DoED |
| Below **1 MW** | **No license required** | — |

**The agency distinction is examined and is worth fixing:**

| Agency | Role |
|---|---|
| **Department of Electricity Development (DoED)** | **LICENSING** — survey and generation licenses; the regulator of project development |
| **Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA)** | The **UTILITY** — generates, transmits, distributes; the **buyer** under a PPA |
| **Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC)** | **Tariff** determination, consumer protection, market regulation (established 2074/2017) |
| **Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation** | Policy |
| **Water and Energy Commission Secretariat (WECS)** | **Planning and study** of water and energy resources |
| **Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC)** | **Micro-hydro** and other rural renewable energy |
| **Investment Board Nepal (IBN)** | Large projects (above a threshold) and PPP structuring |

**So the licensing authority is DoED, not NEA** — a distinction that catches candidates, because NEA is the more visible organisation. NEA is the counterparty to the PPA and the operator of the grid; it does not license.

**The Electricity Regulatory Commission** is the newer body and its creation (2074/2017) marks the separation of **regulation** from **operation** — previously both effectively sat with NEA and the ministry, which is a conflict of interest wherever an incumbent utility also sets the terms for competitors.

**The development sequence** for a private (IPP) project:

1. **Identify** the site and obtain a **survey license**.
2. Conduct **feasibility study** and **environmental assessment (IEE or EIA)**.
3. Obtain **environmental clearance** from the concerned ministry or MoFE.
4. Negotiate and sign the **Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)** with NEA.
5. Obtain the **generation license**.
6. Achieve **financial closure** — equity and debt.
7. **Construct**, commission and begin generation.
8. **Operate** for the license period, then **transfer** to the government (**BOOT**).

**Step 4 before step 5 is the practical reality**: the PPA is what makes the project bankable, so no lender commits and no generation license is meaningfully useful until the offtake is secured.

**The Power Purchase Agreement** is the commercial heart of the project:

| Provision | Significance |
|---|---|
| **Tariff**, with separate **wet and dry season rates** | Dry-season energy is worth more, reflecting the system's winter deficit |
| **Take-or-pay** versus **take-and-pay** | **Take-or-pay obliges the buyer to pay for contracted energy whether taken or not**, transferring market risk to the utility — this is what makes a project bankable |
| Term | Typically matching the license |
| Escalation | Partial indexation, commonly for a limited number of years |
| **Delay damages** and commissioning date | — |
| Force majeure, change in law | Risk allocation |

**Project delivery models:**

| Model | Character |
|---|---|
| **Government (public) development** | NEA or a government company builds and operates |
| **IPP (Independent Power Producer)** | Private developer under a license and PPA |
| **BOOT / BOT** | **Build–Own–Operate–Transfer**: the developer operates for the license term, then **transfers the asset to the government** |
| **PPP** | Various risk-sharing structures |
| **Community / cooperative** | Local ownership; common in micro-hydro and increasingly in small hydro |

**Royalty** is payable to the government under the Electricity Act — a **capacity charge per kW plus an energy charge per kWh**, at rates that are **lower for the first 15 years** of operation and higher thereafter, and lower for smaller plants. A share of the royalty is allocated to the **affected local governments**, which is the mechanism by which the district hosting a project receives a direct benefit — an important provision, since local support depends on local benefit.

**Community benefit sharing** more broadly has become a standard feature: **shares offered to local residents**, local employment obligations, and infrastructure contributions. Its rationale is straightforward and worth stating: a project that imposes local costs (land, disruption, dewatered river) and exports all its benefits will meet local resistance, and the resistance will cost more than the sharing.

sections.heading: Project layout and the environmental release
sections.body:
**The components of a run-of-river scheme**, in the order water passes through them:

> **Diversion weir and intake → Gravel trap → Settling (desilting) basin → Headrace (canal or tunnel) → Forebay or surge tank → Penstock → Powerhouse (turbine, generator) → Tailrace → River**

plus the **transmission line** and **switchyard**, the **access road**, and the **environmental release** at the intake.

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Diversion weir** | Raises the level enough to divert into the intake |
| **Intake** (side or trench weir) | Admits water, excludes floating debris and bed load |
| **Gravel trap** | Catches **coarse bedload** (above about 2 mm) |
| **Settling basin** | Removes particles above the target size (**0.2–0.3 mm**) |
| **Headrace** | Conveys water to the forebay — canal or **tunnel** |
| **Forebay / surge tank** | Short-term storage; ensures **submergence**; absorbs load variation |
| **Penstock** | Carries water **under pressure** to the turbine |
| **Powerhouse** | Turbine, generator, governor, controls |
| **Tailrace** | Returns water to the river |

**Canal or tunnel for the headrace** is a decision worth understanding:

| | **Canal (surface)** | **Tunnel** |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | **Lower** per metre | **Much higher** |
| Alignment | Must follow the contour — **long** | Can be **short and direct** |
| Vulnerability | **Landslides, rockfall, monsoon damage** | Protected |
| Head loss | Higher (longer) | Lower (shorter) |
| Geological risk | Low | **High** — the principal cost risk |
| Maintenance | Regular; accessible | Minimal; hard to access |

**Nepali projects increasingly choose tunnels** despite the cost, because a hillside canal on an unstable slope is a **recurring liability** — damaged in every monsoon, and occasionally destroyed. The tunnel's higher capital cost buys reliability, and the shorter alignment recovers some of it in reduced head loss. The trade is geological risk at construction against operational risk for the plant's life.

**The mandatory environmental release** — a genuine design constraint, not a formality:

> Under the **Electricity Rules** and the project's environmental approval, at least **10% of the minimum monthly average flow**, or the amount specified by the EIA — **whichever is greater** — must be **released continuously** into the river at the intake.

**Its purpose** is to maintain the **dewatered reach** between the intake and the tailrace: aquatic life, downstream domestic and irrigation users, and the river's character.

**Why it is a real constraint** and not a token: the release is deducted from the flow available for generation, and it bites hardest in the **dry season**, when the total flow is least and the energy is most valuable. A scheme on a small stream may find that the release plus the plant's minimum operating flow leaves it unable to generate at all in the driest weeks — which must be recognised in the energy estimate rather than discovered afterwards.

The **dewatered reach** is the length of river between the intake and the tailrace, and it can be several kilometres in a scheme with a long tunnel. Its condition is the most visible environmental effect of a run-of-river plant, and it is what the release exists to mitigate.

**Selecting the layout — the trade-offs:**

| Decision | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| **Intake location** | Higher gives more head but a longer conveyance and worse access |
| **Design flow** | A higher design flow gives more capacity but a lower **plant factor**, since the river seldom supplies it |
| **Headrace length** | Longer gives more head but more cost and loss |
| **Powerhouse location** | Must be above the flood level but as low as possible for head |
| **Surface or underground powerhouse** | Underground costs more but is safe from **rockfall, landslide and flood** |
| **Settling basin size** | Larger removes finer particles but costs more and takes land |

**The design flow decision is the central economic choice**, and it is where the flow duration curve does its work:

> A **higher design flow** means a **larger plant** that generates more in the monsoon but stands partly idle for much of the year — a **lower plant factor** and a higher cost per unit of energy.
> A **lower design flow** means a **smaller plant** operating near capacity most of the time — a higher plant factor, but the monsoon surplus is spilled unused.

The optimum is found by computing the **energy and cost for a range of design flows** and selecting the one giving the **lowest levelised cost** or the highest net present value. In Nepali practice the design flow is conventionally taken around **Q₄₀** — the flow exceeded 40% of the time — but that is a starting point for the optimisation, not a rule.

**Powerhouse siting** deserves a final note for Himalayan conditions. A powerhouse must be above the design flood level, clear of **landslide and rockfall** paths, and clear of **debris flow** fans at tributary mouths — the last being easy to overlook, because a debris fan looks like a convenient flat site and is in fact the deposit of the very event that would destroy the building on it. **Underground (cavern) powerhouses** avoid all three hazards and are increasingly chosen for medium and large Nepali projects for that reason.

formulas.label: Nepal capacity classification
formulas.expression: micro < 100 kW ; mini 100 kW–1 MW ; small 1–25 MW ; medium 25–100 MW ; large > 100 MW
formulas.note: Below 1 MW no survey or generation license is required — a deliberate simplification for small schemes.

formulas.label: License durations
formulas.expression: survey license 5 years ; generation license up to 35 years (30 with foreign investment)
formulas.note: Both issued by the Department of Electricity Development (DoED) — NOT by NEA, which is the utility and buyer.

formulas.label: Water use priority (Water Resources Act 2049)
formulas.expression: 1 drinking/domestic · 2 irrigation · 3 agricultural · 4 HYDROPOWER · 5 industrial · 6 navigation · 7 recreation
formulas.note: Hydropower ranks fourth, so existing drinking water and irrigation intakes hold a prior right.

formulas.label: Mandatory environmental release
formulas.expression: at least 10% of the minimum monthly average flow, or the EIA requirement — whichever is GREATER
formulas.note: Released continuously at the intake to maintain the dewatered reach. Bites hardest in the dry season.

formulas.label: Study stage cost accuracy
formulas.note: Each stage spends more to reduce uncertainty; the discipline is to abandon weak schemes early.

formulas.label: Settling basin target particle size
formulas.expression: remove particles above about 0.2 to 0.3 mm; gravel trap catches above about 2 mm
formulas.note: Abrasive Himalayan quartz above ~0.2 mm is what destroys turbine runners.

formulas.label: Design flow selection
formulas.expression: Conventionally around Q₄₀ (exceeded 40% of the time), optimised for lowest levelised cost
formulas.note: A higher design flow gives more capacity but a lower plant factor. It is an optimisation, not a rule.
